wheat.lead: Wheat plants, grain products, harvest crafts and classroom activities.
wheat.heading: Choose wheat artwork for the story you want to tell
paragraphs: A single grain head gives a small card a clear silhouette, while the rooted plants show a different part of the crop. The collection separates germination, young leaves, side shoots, stem nodes, heading and flowering. Wheat is a grass: its long leaves and compact spikelets differ from the branching panicles of oats or the broad leaves of a garden vegetable. The detached spikelet and kernel views can sit beside a whole plant in an observation activity. Add your own labels in the editor; the illustrations do not contain a preprinted diagram.

For a food-themed page, follow the visible ingredients and objects rather than treating every grain product as interchangeable. The sieve holds kernels and chaff, the small mill releases flour, the bowl of bran shows papery flakes, and the clear jar contains cracked grain. Separate baking compositions show sifting, dough, a round scored loaf, cut bread and dry pasta. These are useful visual prompts for a personal recipe notebook or a classroom vocabulary display. They are illustrations of materials and processes, not recipes, dietary advice or engineering instructions.

Straw also appears as a craft material. Choose a plaited ornament, a tied star, a woven hat, hollow stalk segments or a wreath with a clear center. The wax seal, embroidered felt brooch, pressed nature journal and biscuit stamp each have a different purpose and construction. Use the open corner spray at the edge of a card, keep a wreath center available for a short message, or pair the wrapped bouquet with a personal thank-you caption. Leave delicate awns and threads enough space to remain visible.

The six outline designs depict separate activities: binding a cut bundle, weighing grain, rolling dough, storing a crop, embroidering a motif and observing roots. They are independent compositions rather than outlined copies of the color pictures. In the online editor you can move, resize and rotate the drawing, add text and shapes, and save an editable project. A bottle, pitcher, spoon, breakfast or small maple candy composition can support a personal recipe page or a classroom discussion about products made from sap. These pictures show visible objects and settings, not equipment instructions, food labels or a claim about a particular brand.

For a decorative layout, choose an open frame, corner, border or wreath and keep your words in the clear space. The felt ornament, carved wooden leaf and framed leaf offer different craft materials. cranberry.heading: Find cranberry artwork for a menu, lesson or craft
paragraphs: For a nature activity, choose the view that makes the detail easy to observe. A rooted runner shows the low woody stem, small leafy shoots and berries at different stages of ripening. The flowering stem has pale pink blossoms with recurved petals, while a nursery plant has an exposed root plug beside its pot. A cut-fruit study shows four hollow chambers beside a magnifying glass. Another arrangement pairs floating whole berries with a cut half on a saucer. Place your own labels outside the small roots, petals and cut surfaces so the details remain readable.

The harvest scenes show different jobs. A farmer in waders gathers floating berries with a long rake inside a curved boom. A kneeling picker works beside dry low vines, and a worker sorts red and pale fruit between two trays. At the market stand, a silver-braided seller holds a paper bag beneath a teal awning. The handcart carries shallow harvest crates and work gloves. These images work well as sequence cards, observation prompts and farm vocabulary pictures. The water scene represents harvesting; it does not show cranberries growing permanently underwater.

Sauces and storage arrangements make useful kitchen vocabulary images. Choose an open whole-berry sauce jar, a copper saucepan, a crock of cranberry-orange chutney or sliced cranberry jelly on a serving platter. Other drawings show fruit being rinsed in a colander, weighed on a kitchen scale, measured in an enamel cup, frozen in a zipper bag or dried in a paper pouch. The juice pitcher, sparkling drink, fruit-filled ice cubes and frozen-pop mold have different container shapes and purposes. Use what is visibly pictured when writing a menu caption, rather than treating an illustration as a tested recipe.

For a baking page, the collection includes triangular scones, muffins with an open crumb view, sliced quick bread, cheesecake, an upside-down cake, biscotti and a tall frosted layer cake. Savory food scenes include cranberry-topped crostini, soft baked brie, leafy salad, a cut turkey sandwich, herb stuffing and roasted Brussels sprouts. Granola, trail mix and a layered yogurt glass offer separate breakfast and snack arrangements. Match the shape to your layout: a tall jar fits beside a short paragraph, a roasting pan spans a wider area, and a single dessert wedge suits a compact menu card.

Seasonal craft details include a preserve gift with a blank tag, a cranberry-and-popcorn string, a vine wreath, a linen napkin ring and an open botanical plant press. The L-shaped vine corner leaves space for your own wording. Playful fruit characters and different whole-and-cut fruit treatments provide additional choices for personal stationery and classroom activities. Independent outline scenes show family baking, harvest equipment, a crane beside a cranberry-water patch, frozen pops and sweet rolls. Choose the actual drawing that fits the activity instead of making a small fruit image carry too much text.

In the editor you can move, resize and rotate the artwork, add editable text and shapes, and save a project for later. Each detailed painting or outline composition is one image layer; the berries, leaves, clothing, utensil parts and individual strokes are not separate vector pieces. Keep small seeds, thin plant stems and fine tableware details large enough for the intended page. Keep your labels outside the small roots and veins so that the illustration remains readable.

The garden scenes offer different actions and scales. A bearded gardener supports a tall stem, a curly-haired child holds a measuring stick, and a silver-haired gardener carries a cut flower beside a red bucket. A small finch perches below a spent seed head, while a butterfly appears beside a fresh blossom and a ladybird rests on a leaf below a closed bud. The field vignette has rows behind a wooden gate. These drawings can support observation prompts without assigning an exact cultivar, plant age or height that the picture cannot establish.

Choose a floral arrangement by the space available on the page. A wrapped bouquet has a compact diagonal shape, a single flower in a narrow glass bottle is tall, and a market bucket forms a wider cluster. The grapevine wreath and wire heart frame leave open centers for a short personal message. The botanical corner and hanging garland fit along page edges. A florist crate, a decorated straw hat and a sunflower-shaped foil balloon give gift and celebration layouts their own objects rather than repeating one bouquet.

The craft illustrations show different materials clearly: folded paper petals, stitched felt, thick crochet yarn, joined stained glass, embroidery on navy linen, a small pendant, fabric applique and a tiled coaster. A wooden stamp appears with its ink impression, while the pressed specimen card, cloth notebook and long bookmark suit nature-journal and reading activities. The seed drawings include a divided sorting tray, a paper packet, shelled kernels, an oil cruet, seed-topped bread, a jar of spread and a hanging bird feeder. Use the visible objects as vocabulary pictures or personal design accents.

Separate black-and-white compositions show children watering, a garden fence, a seated flower-crown maker, four growth stages, a photographer and an open bookplate frame. school.heading: Choose a school scene for your page
paragraphs: A backpack, yellow bus or school building reads clearly on a label or invitation. Let larger scenes such as playground recess or a classroom activity occupy more space so the people and objects remain visible.

Pair reading and library artwork with a short book title or reading goal. Science-class and teacher scenes suit classroom newsletters and lesson headings. Keep separate captions outside the detailed illustration.

The black-and-white versions are useful when color printing is unavailable or children will add their own marks. Preview each design at its final size, then arrange it with editable text and shapes in Clipart Studio.
school.print: Every school design includes a transparent 1,500 × 1,500 WebP and a matching 2-inch-square CMYK PDF containing a 1,500 × 1,500 image. Six WebPs in the supplied ZIP were empty or had mismatched transparency; the published copies were reconstructed from their matching PDFs and checked against the PDF renders.

smart-doorbell.heading: Smart doorbell illustrations for entrances, devices and everyday visits
paragraphs: An isolated camera doorbell keeps attention on the lens, call button and speaker. Slim units, round intercoms, decorative bronze plates and a three-button apartment panel provide different recognizable forms for a device comparison or a personal home-planning page.

Entrance scenes show siding, stucco, stone, a garden gate and a shared pair of front doors. A parcel bench, wet steps and a snowy porch add specific context to a layout. Match the entrance and weather to the story you want to tell instead of reusing the same background for every project.

Visitor illustrations include a courier, a person carrying flowers, a dog walker, an older grocery shopper and a wheelchair user reaching a call button. Indoor scenes show answering a visitor on a phone and using a separate video receiver. These compositions can support classroom discussions of everyday technology and accessible entrances.

The parts illustrations show a mounting plate, angled bracket, removable battery, chime, camera board and front housing. The exploded view is a generic educational reference; the construction and wiring of individual devices vary. The outline versions provide a simpler choice for personal worksheets.
Use transparent WebP in digital layouts or the matching CMYK PDF in print projects. The editor keeps the original illustration as one intact layer while the text and shapes you add remain separate.
smart-doorbell.print: Each standard PDF is checked for a real four-channel CMYK image, a registered GRACoL print output condition, matching artwork and a file size below 1,000,000 bytes. Transparent WebP preserves the exported source pixels. Keep the artwork in its original proportions and choose a print size suited to its resolution.

labubu.heading: Choose the Labubu expression and activity that fits your page
paragraphs: Labubu is the mischievous, kind-hearted forest elf created by artist Kasing Lung for THE MONSTERS. The character’s long pointed ears, expressive oval eyes and distinctive nine-tooth grin give it a recognizable silhouette even in a small composition. This collection focuses on that character identity through different activities, rather than repeating one pose in a row of colors. The illustrations are independent fan-art scenes; they do not represent named collectible editions or an official POP MART collaboration.

For a personal birthday card or gift tag, try the cupcake, wrapped present, party balloons or cheerful waving pose. Leave room beside the ears for a short greeting instead of covering the face. The heart, bouquet, envelope and sunflower compositions suit a personal thank-you note or a message to a friend. A full standing figure works well beside a paragraph; a seated pose creates a quieter focal point near the bottom of a page.

For a reading journal or classroom activity, choose a visible action that supports your message: reading a book, carrying a book stack, painting, watering a seedling, observing a butterfly or holding a reward star. Match the picture to the activity instead of using a decorative character as a substitute for instructions. The six coloring drawings introduce different scenes with larger open spaces: a little detective, block building, a laundry basket, a paper boat, a rocking horse and a pumpkin wheelbarrow. Use the picture beside your own question, routine or creative prompt.

For seasonal pages, choose the umbrella, picnic, seaside bucket, autumn leaves, snowball, warm mug or holiday gift sack. Keep small props large enough to recognize at the final size. In the editor you can move, resize and rotate the illustration, add text or shapes, and arrange a personal card or worksheet. The illustrated character remains a single image layer; save your editable project if you want to return to the layout later.
labubu.print: Each design has a transparent WebP and a matching four-channel CMYK PDF below 1,000,000 bytes. The PDF references a registered GRACoL output condition; the complete ICC profile is not embedded. Check the artwork page for the actual PDF dimensions at 300 pixels per inch. The native WebP retains the larger original canvas. Leave enough space for the small teeth, fur edges and fine outline details, and check a sample at your intended print size.

Use an outline for a coloring activity or choose a complete scene when its setting carries your message. gratitude.description: Explore gratitude clipart with thoughtful gestures, helpful people, family moments and classroom crafts. Download transparent WebP and matching CMYK PDF files.
gratitude.intro: Find a thoughtful scene for a personal thank-you card, reflection journal, classroom discussion or community-helper activity. The collection includes ordinary acts of kindness, people showing appreciation, handmade gifts and quiet moments of reflection. Each design has a transparent WebP, a matching CMYK PDF and an online editor for your own layout.
gratitude.lead: Everyday kindness, appreciation and thoughtful classroom activities.
gratitude.heading: Choose a gratitude scene for a card, journal or lesson
paragraphs: Start with the action you want to discuss. A child sharing a pencil, a sister tying a younger child's shoe and two friends sharing an umbrella each give a clear example of practical help. Ask learners to describe what they can actually see before adding their own reason for saying thank you. The book-sharing scene and the pair reading together also work beside a short writing prompt about friendship. Keep the hands, faces and shared object visible when placing the scene on a page.

For a school appreciation activity, choose a helper and a matching gesture. A child offers a card to a bus driver with keys at her waist. A girl gives daisies to a custodian holding a broom, while a librarian receives a leaf bookmark beside a stack of books. Other drawings show a lunch worker offering a tray, a crossing helper beside a child with a backpack, and an art coach sharing a high five. These are individual illustrated scenes; add your own names or message in the editor rather than treating the people as a real school's staff.

Family and neighborhood scenes provide different ways to show appreciation. A grandfather and child share a hug beside a bench. Neighbors exchange bread or a covered casserole, and an older person receives soup from a volunteer. A friend gives a wrapped parcel to someone seated in a wheelchair. Another scene shows a parent thanking a child for help with folded laundry. Use the complete interaction in a personal card, a classroom story sequence or a discussion about noticing helpful actions. Avoid cropping away the prop that explains the exchange.

For a quieter reflection page, try the seated journal writer, the woman reading a letter, the man making a phone call or the child with one hand over the chest. A grandmother sits quietly on a wooden bench, and a grandfather shares an album with a listening child. The family raising water glasses gives a separate group scene for discussing shared moments. Leave a clear writing area beside the illustration so a learner or card recipient can add their own words. The pictures suggest prompts and do not provide a personal story on anyone's behalf.

Handmade arrangements suit practical classroom activities and personal stationery. The paper chain has linked colored loops, a glue stick and a spare strip. The fabric wall organizer has three pockets with heart cards, and the pencil pot carries painted flowers and a blank heart tag. A keepsake box holds small papers and a ribbon. A decorated picture frame, an open scrapbook and painted reflection stones offer other ways to organize a memory page. The cookie gift box is a separate food arrangement. Choose the object that matches the planned activity, then add an editable caption outside its fine details.

The outline scenes have their own compositions for coloring and discussion. A gardener and child carry a seedling tray, a child presents a heart picture on an easel, and a bundled helper stands beside a neighbor with a snow shovel. Other drawings show a paper-kite craft, a journal picnic and two reading partners on a bench. Keep small fingers, seedlings, shoelaces and craft tools large enough for the chosen print size. A few simple questions beside one complete scene can be easier to use than a crowded page of tiny drawings.

Open a design in the editor to move, resize, rotate or crop it, add separate editable text and shape layers, and save the project for later. Each detailed illustration is one image layer; the people, clothing, props and individual painted strokes are not separate vector pieces. Use a contrasting background if pale paper, white flowers or light clothing becomes difficult to see. The site license covers personal and educational use. Commercial use and resale as clipart are prohibited.
gratitude.print: Each design includes a transparent WebP and a matching CMYK PDF below 1,000,000 bytes. The artwork page gives its actual image dimensions and stated print size. WebP files preserve the native illustration pixels; the PDF uses its declared 300-pixel-per-inch print dimensions. Print at actual size for that scale, keep delicate lines readable, and check a sample when choosing paper or a larger layout.

diwali.lead: Diyas, rangoli, sweets and shared preparations for cards and learning activities.
diwali.heading: Choose a Diwali illustration for a greeting, craft or classroom page
paragraphs: Begin with the object or activity your page needs to explain. A single clay diya leaves room for a short greeting, while a stepped stand with five lamps makes a wider arrangement. The lotus-shaped lamp has layered metal petals and a stable base. For a window or entrance layout, choose the blue-shuttered window or the complete double doorway with flowers, lamps and a petal pattern on its steps. Keep the wick, flame and supporting surface visible when placing a lamp illustration; these details help distinguish an oil lamp from a candle or a paper decoration.

The rangoli designs offer different kinds of pattern work. The circular peacock arrangement has a scalloped edge and a blue bird at its center. Another picture shows a woman making a quarter-circle floral design beside bowls of colored material. A mother and child arrange a flower-star pattern with petal bowls and a basket. The separate outline lesson uses a square-and-diamond composition. These can sit beside an observation prompt about shape, repetition or color. Keep the complete pattern visible and leave a separate space for a learner's own response rather than placing writing over the small details.

For classroom craft pages, choose illustrations showing paper materials. The folded red paper diya has a layered paper flame, scissors, glue and spare strips. The lantern kit has a partly folded purple decoration, a ruler, a pencil and a star punch. A hanging mobile carries four paper lamps with beads and tassels. Other scenes show a teacher and children making lanterns, a child assembling a paper-leaf toran, and a family decorating a window. Paper flames represent craft pieces. Keep these examples distinct from drawings of real lit lamps when explaining what the pictured activity involves.

Sweets and gifts suit personal menus, greeting cards and festival vocabulary pages. The divided mithai box contains round orange sweets, pale diamonds and orange spirals. Separate arrangements show a footed dish of ladoo, a leaf-lined platter of diamond sweets and jalebi on a blue-and-white plate. A drawstring pouch with nuts and dried fruit provides a different gift composition. Food illustrations show appearance rather than a recipe, ingredient list or allergen information. Use your own checked labels if a page describes actual food you plan to serve.

The people scenes show different preparations and shared activities. A woman paints an unlit diya at a low table, a man and child thread marigolds, and a potter shapes a lamp on a manual wheel. A father hangs a lantern from a porch beam while a child holds its tassel. Neighbors share sweets at a decorated doorway, family members greet with palms together, and an older woman reads a lamp-themed book to a child. Select the action that supports your story or lesson. The drawings are individual examples and do not represent every family's customs or a single required way of celebrating.

The outline illustrations are separate compositions for coloring and discussion. They include polishing an unlit lamp, serving sweets at a decorated counter, making a paper toran, arranging rangoli, decorating a window and packing a divided gift box. Use one complete scene at a comfortable size so hands, tools and small decorative shapes remain clear. Add a short observation question or a blank writing area beside it. For a personal invitation, the open greeting card and envelope provide an alternative with an uncluttered space for your own message.

Open a design in the editor to move, resize, rotate or crop it, add editable text and shapes, and save the project for later. Each detailed painting is one image layer; its people, garments, lamps and brushstrokes are not separate vector parts. Try a contrasting background when pale fabric, white paper or light flowers need more definition. Personal and educational use is permitted under the site license. Commercial use and resale as clipart are prohibited.
